faq.a: AVPU is rapid for triage; GCS provides detailed grading once the patient is stabilized.
faq.q: Why use AVPU when GCS is available?

faq.a: Yes; focal deficits or abnormal pupils can indicate serious pathology despite normal AVPU.
faq.q: Can a patient be alert but still have serious brain injury?

faq.a: Intravenous artesunate is first‑line; it rapidly clears parasites and improves consciousness.
faq.q: What is the first drug to give for suspected cerebral malaria?

exam: A 7‑year‑old with fever and a GCS of 9 – what immediate steps do you take? — Secure airway if GCS ≤8, give oxygen, check glucose, start antimalarial if rapid test positive, obtain malaria smear.
A patient presents with a GCS of 6, pinpoint pupils, and a history of opioid use – what is the most likely diagnosis and management? — Opioid overdose; give naloxone while protecting airway.
How does West‑Haven grading differ from GCS in assessing encephalopathy? — West‑Haven focuses on consciousness alone (1‑4); GCS adds eye, verbal, motor components, giving finer prognostic detail.

In a malaria‑endemic area, a comatose patient has a normal glucose and negative malaria test – what are the next three investigations? — Check serum electrolytes, perform lumbar puncture if safe, obtain CT head if available.
Why is ketamine avoided in a patient with suspected raised intracranial pressure? — Ketamine can increase cerebral blood flow and ICP, worsening herniation risk.
A patient with severe hyponatraemia is confused but has a GCS of 14 – how does this affect your management? — Treat hyponatraemia slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination; monitor GCS for deterioration.
What red‑flag sign on pupil examination mandates immediate neurosurgical review? — Fixed, dilated, non‑reactive pupil indicating possible uncal herniation.
Explain why a normal capillary refill does not rule out early septic shock. — Early shock may preserve peripheral perfusion; look for warm skin, tachycardia, and altered mental status.
ai.title: Level of Consciousness Assessment
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Level of consciousness (LOC) reflects brain function and guides urgent management. Clinicians use bedside scales, identify reversible causes, and stage severity to predict outcome, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: AVPU is quick: any response below Alert signals altered LOC.
GCS scores 3–15; ≤8 indicates severe impairment needing airway protection.
sections.p: LOC describes a patient’s arousal, awareness, and ability to interact. It is assessed at the bedside with the AVPU scale (Alert, Voice, Pain, Unresponsive) and the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS).

t.b: Is the patient alert, responsive to voice, pain, or unresponsive? – Determines need for immediate airway support and urgency of further work‑up.
What is the numeric score of eye, verbal, and motor responses? – Scores ≤8 suggest severe encephalopathy; 9‑12 moderate; 13‑15 mild.

b: West‑Haven 1: Normal consciousness.
West‑Haven 4: Coma, no response to pain.
sections.p: Beyond AVPU, the West‑Haven grade (1‑4) and GCS provide prognostic staging for encephalopathy and traumatic brain injury.

b: Infections: cerebral malaria, bacterial meningitis, tuberculous meningitis, HIV‑related opportunistic infections.
Metabolic: severe hypoglycaemia, hyperglycaemic crisis, hyponatraemia, renal failure uremia, hepatic encephalopathy.
Toxins: herbal preparations, organophosphates, alcohol withdrawal.
Vascular: large hemispheric stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage, raised intracranial pressure.
sections.p: In East African low‑resource hospitals, common reversible causes dominate: infections, metabolic derangements, toxins, and structural brain lesions.

b: Rapid breathing and warm skin suggest sepsis‑related lactic acidosis.
Cold, clammy skin with delayed capillary refill (>3 s) points to shock.
sections.p: Patients may be drowsy, confused, agitated, or unresponsive. Look for associated signs: fever, neck stiffness, focal deficits, skin colour, capillary refill, and pupil reactivity.
Prioritise bedside and low‑cost tests that answer specific questions about the cause of altered LOC.

t.b: Is hypoglycaemia present? – <2.8 mmol/L confirms need for immediate dextrose.
Is peripheral perfusion adequate? – >3 s suggests shock, prompting fluid resuscitation.

t.a: Full blood count & malaria rapid test
t.b: Is malaria or severe infection likely? – Positive malaria test directs antimalarial therapy.

t.a: Serum electrolytes & renal function (if lab available)
t.b: Are metabolic derangements present? – Correcting sodium, potassium, urea, or creatinine can reverse encephalopathy.
Is meningitis present? – CSF pleocytosis, low glucose, high protein guide antimicrobial choice.
Is there a structural lesion or raised ICP? – Detects bleed, mass effect, hydrocephalus; guides neurosurgical referral.
Is a toxin suspected? – Positive result directs specific antidote or decontamination.

b: GCS ≤8 or West‑Haven 4 – airway protection needed.
Pupillary asymmetry or non‑reactive pupils – possible brain herniation.
Seizures or new focal deficit – risk of permanent injury.
Airway: If GCS ≤8, perform jaw thrust, insert oropharyngeal airway, and consider endotracheal intubation with rapid sequence induction (avoid ketamine in raised ICP).
Breathing: Give supplemental oxygen; treat seizures with benzodiazepines (e.g., diazepam) – avoid long‑acting barbiturates in hepatic failure.
Circulation: Give isotonic crystalloid bolus (e.g., normal saline) for shock; monitor capillary refill.
Specific causes: Give IV dextrose for hypoglycaemia; start antimalarials for confirmed malaria; administer broad‑spectrum antibiotics for meningitis; correct electrolytes cautiously.
Avoid: High‑dose phenobarbital in hepatic encephalopathy; NSAIDs in renal failure; sedatives in raised ICP.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care to protect the airway, optimise perfusion, and prevent secondary injury.

b: Educate patients on malaria prophylaxis, HIV treatment adherence, and safe herbal use.
Arrange follow‑up for chronic diseases (diabetes, hypertension) that predispose to metabolic encephalopathy.
sections.p: Re‑assess GCS hourly until stable. Identify and modify chronic risk factors.

b: Severe fatigue – patient is awake but low energy; LOC scales remain normal.
Psychiatric agitation – consciousness intact; focus on thought content rather than arousal.
sections.p: Altered LOC can mimic other acute presentations.

b: Normal capillary refill in early shock – may be misleading if ambient temperature is warm.
Normal glucose in a patient on high‑dose insulin – consider recent insulin administration; repeat test.
sections.p: Certain bedside findings may be falsely reassuring.

whenToSeekHelp: Seizure lasting >5 minutes or recurrent seizures
